Main.sentence: Paul Davis Ryan (born January 29, 1970) is an American politician who served as the ___E:54th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Speakers_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ ___E:speaker of the United States House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ from 2015 to 2019. A member of the ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ , he was the party's ___E:vice presidential U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States)___ nominee in the ___E:2012 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election)___ running alongside ___E:Mitt Romney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney)___ , losing to President ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ and Vice President ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ .

Ryan is a native of ___E:Janesville, Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janesville,_Wisconsin)___ , and graduated from ___E:Miami University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_University)___ in 1992. He spent five years working for Congress in Washington, D.C., becoming a speechwriter, then returned to Wisconsin in 1997 to work at his family's construction company.

He was elected to Congress to represent Wisconsin's 1st congressional district the following year, replacing ___E:Mark Neumann U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Neumann)___ , who had vacated the seat to run for U.S.
Senate.
Ryan went on to represent the district for 20 years.

He chaired the ___E:House Budget Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_the_Budget)___ from 2011 to 2015, and briefly chaired the ___E:House Ways and Means Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Ways_and_Means)___ in 2015.

A self-proclaimed ___E:deficit hawk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deficit_hawk)___ , Ryan was a major proponent of ___E:Social Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States))___ privatization in the mid-2000s.

During the 2010s, two proposals heavily influenced by Ryan—" ___E:The Path to Prosperity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Path_to_Prosperity)___ " and " ___E:A Better Way U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Better_Way)___ "—became part of the national dialogue advocating for the privatization of ___E:Medicare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States))___ , the conversion of ___E:Medicaid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid_(United_States))___ into a ___E:block grant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_grant)___ program, the repeal of the ___E:Affordable Care Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act)___ , and significant federal tax cuts. In October 2015, after Speaker ___E:John Boehner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner)___ 's resignation, Ryan was ___E:elected to replace him U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2015_Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives_election)___ .

During his speakership, he played a key role in the passage of the ___E:Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Cuts_and_Jobs_Act_of_2017)___ and the ___E:Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief and Consumer Protection Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Growth,_Regulatory_Relief_and_Consumer_Protection_Act)___ in 2018, which partially repealed the ___E:Dodd–Frank Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodd%E2%80%93Frank_Wall_Street_Reform_and_Consumer_Protection_Act)___ .
Ryan declined to run for re-election in the ___E:2018 midterm elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections)___ .

With the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ taking control of the House of Representatives, ___E:Nancy Pelosi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi)___ succeeded Ryan as Speaker of the House.

Paul Davis Ryan was born on January 29, 1970, in ___E:Janesville, Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janesville,_Wisconsin)___ , the youngest of four children of Elizabeth "Betty" Ann, who later became an interior designer, and Paul Murray Ryan, a lawyer.
He is a fifth-generation Wisconsinite.

His father was of ___E:Irish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_American)___ ancestry and his mother of ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_American)___ and ___E:English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_American)___ descent.
One of Ryan's paternal ancestors settled in Wisconsin prior to the ___E:Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ .
His great-grandfather, Patrick William Ryan, founded an ___E:earthmoving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_equipment_(construction))___ company in 1884, which later became P. W.
Ryan and Sons and is now known as Ryan Incorporated Central.

Ryan's grandfather, Stanley M. Ryan, was appointed ___E:United States Attorney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney)___ for the ___E:Western District of Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Western_District_of_Wisconsin)___ .

In 2018, while filming a segment for the PBS series Finding Your Roots , Ryan learned that his DNA results included 3 percent ___E:Ashkenazi Jewish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jew)___ ancestry.

Ryan attended St. Mary's Catholic School in Janesville, then attended ___E:Joseph A. Craig High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_A._Craig_High_School)___ ,  where he was elected president of his junior class, and thus became ___E:prom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prom)___ king.  As class president Ryan was a representative of the student body on the ___E:school board U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_board)___ .
Following his second year, Ryan took a job working the grill at ___E:McDonald's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald%27s)___ .

He was on his high school's ___E:ski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiing)___ , track, and ___E:varsity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varsity_team)___ soccer teams and played ___E:basketball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball)___ in a Catholic recreational league.
He participated in several academic and social clubs including the ___E:Model United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_United_Nations)___ .

Ryan and his family often went on hiking and ___E:skiing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiing)___ trips to the ___E:Colorado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado)___ ___E:Rocky Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains)___ .
Although Ryan's father was not a lifelong heavy drinker, staying sober for nearly twenty years after his first stint in rehabilitation, he had become an alcoholic by the time Ryan was a teenager.

Ryan later commented on his relationship with his father, whom he revered as a young child, stating that "[alcohol] made him more distant, irritable and stressed ... whiskey had washed away some of the best parts of the man I knew."  When he was 16, Ryan found his 55-year-old father lying dead in bed of a heart attack, something Ryan later partially attributed to heavy alcohol consumption.
Following the death of his father, Ryan's grandmother moved in with the family.
As she had ___E:Alzheimer's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alzheimer%27s_disease)___ , Ryan helped care for her while his mother commuted to college in Madison, Wisconsin.

From the time of his father's death until his 18th birthday, Ryan received ___E:Social Security survivors benefits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States)#Children's_benefits)___ which were saved for his college education.
His mother later married widower Bruce Douglas.

Ryan has a bachelor's degree in ___E:economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics)___ and ___E:political science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science)___ from ___E:Miami University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_University)___ in ___E:Oxford, Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford,_Ohio)___ ,  where he became interested in the writings of ___E:Friedrich Hayek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek)___ , ___E:Ludwig von Mises U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises)___ , and ___E:Milton Friedman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman)___ .

He often visited the office of ___E:libertarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism_in_the_United_States)___ professor Richard Hart to discuss the theories of these economists and of ___E:Ayn Rand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayn_Rand)___ .
Hart introduced Ryan to National Review ,  and with Hart's recommendation Ryan began an ___E:internship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internship)___ in the D.C. office of Wisconsin U.S.
Senator ___E:Bob Kasten U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Kasten)___ , where he worked with Kasten's foreign affairs adviser.
Ryan attended the Washington Semester program at ___E:American University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_University)___ .
He worked summers as a salesman for ___E:Oscar Mayer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Mayer)___ and once got to drive the ___E:Wienermobile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wienermobile)___ .

Ryan was a member of the ___E:College Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Republicans)___ ,  and volunteered for the congressional campaign of ___E:John Boehner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner)___ .

He was a member of the ___E:Delta Tau Delta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Tau_Delta)___ social ___E:fraternity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraternities_and_sororities_in_North_America)___ .

Betty Ryan reportedly urged her son to accept a congressional position as a legislative aide in Senator Kasten's office, which he did after graduating in 1992.    In his early years working on ___E:Capitol Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Hill)___ , Ryan supplemented his income by working as a waiter, as a fitness trainer, and at other jobs.

A few months after Kasten lost to Democrat ___E:Russ Feingold U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russ_Feingold)___ in the ___E:1992 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_Wisconsin,_1992)___ , Ryan became a ___E:speechwriter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speechwriter)___ for Empower America (which later became ___E:FreedomWorks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FreedomWorks)___ ), a conservative advocacy group founded by ___E:Jack Kemp U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kemp)___ , ___E:Jeane Kirkpatrick U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeane_Kirkpatrick)___ , and ___E:William Bennett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bennett)___ .

Ryan later worked as a speechwriter for Kemp,  the Republican vice presidential candidate in the ___E:1996 United States presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election)___ .
Kemp became Ryan's mentor, and Ryan has said he had a "huge influence".
In 1995, Ryan became the legislative director for then-U.S.
Congressman ___E:Sam Brownback U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Brownback)___ of ___E:Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas)___ .

In 1997 he returned to Wisconsin and worked for a year as a ___E:marketing consultant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing)___ for the ___E:construction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construction)___ company Ryan Incorporated Central, owned by his relatives.

Ryan was first elected to the House in 1998, winning the 1st District seat of Republican ___E:Mark Neumann U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Neumann)___ , a two-term incumbent who had vacated his seat to make an unsuccessful bid for the U.S.

Senate. 28-year-old Ryan won the Republican primary over 29-year-old pianist Michael J. Logan of ___E:Twin Lakes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Lakes,_Wisconsin)___ ,  and the general election against ___E:Democrat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:Lydia Spottswood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Spottswood)___ .
This made him the second-youngest member of the House.
Reelected eight times, Ryan never received less than 55 percent of the vote in a congressional election.
He defeated Democratic challenger ___E:Jeffrey C. Thomas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_C._Thomas)___ in the 2000, 2002, 2004, and 2006 elections.
In the ___E:2008 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Wisconsin,_2008#District_1)___ , Ryan defeated Democrat Marge Krupp.

In the ___E:2010 general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Wisconsin,_2010#District_1)___ , he defeated Democrat John Heckenlively and Libertarian Joseph Kexel.

In 2012, under Wisconsin ___E:election law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_law)___ , Ryan was allowed to run concurrently for vice president and for Congress  and was not allowed to remove his name from the Congressional ballot after being nominated for the vice presidency.
He faced Democratic nominee Rob Zerban.
As of July 25, 2012, Ryan had over $5.4 million in his congressional campaign account, more than any other House member.
He was reelected with 55 percent of his district's vote  and 44 percent of the vote in his hometown, Janesville.
Zerban again challenged Ryan in the ___E:2014 House election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Wisconsin,_2014)___ .
Ryan won with 63 percent of his district's vote.

In the 2016 Republican primary election, Ryan faced businessman ___E:Paul Nehlen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nehlen)___ , who had been endorsed by ___E:Sarah Palin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Palin)___ .

Because of Nehlen's support for Trump, Trump publicly thanked him on Twitter and later told The Washington Post that Nehlen was "running a very good campaign", even though he did not endorse him.    On August 5, 2016, Trump endorsed Ryan's re-election after pressure from fellow Republican leaders.

In the primary election on August 9, 2016,  Ryan overwhelmingly defeated Nehlen, taking over 84 percent of the vote.  In the November general election, Ryan faced Democrat Rebecca Solen  and won with 65 percent of his district's vote.
Committee assignments
As Speaker of the House of Representatives, Ryan was not a chair or a member of any committee.
Prior to his speakership, Ryan held the following assignments:
Caucus memberships

Ryan became the ranking Republican member of the ___E:House Budget Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Budget_Committee)___ in 2007  and became chairman of the committee in 2011 after Republicans took control of the House.
That same year, he was selected to deliver the ___E:Republican response to the State of the Union address U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_response_to_the_State_of_the_Union_address)___ .

As of August 2012, Ryan had been the primary sponsor of more than 70 ___E:bills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_(proposed_law))___ or amendments,   and only two of those bills had become law.  One, passed in July 2000, renamed a post office in Ryan's district; the other, passed in December 2008, lowered the ___E:excise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excise)___ tax on ___E:arrow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow)___ shafts.
As of August 2012, Ryan had also co-sponsored 975 bills, of which 176 had passed; 22% of these bills were originally sponsored by a Democrat.

Ryan was a "reliable supporter of the [George W. Bush] administration's foreign policy priorities" who voted for the 2002 ___E:Iraq Resolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Resolution)___ , authorizing the ___E:2003 invasion of Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq)___ .

In 2010, Ryan was a member of the bipartisan ___E:National Commission on Fiscal Responsibility and Reform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Commission_on_Fiscal_Responsibility_and_Reform)___ (Bowles-Simpson Commission), which was tasked with developing a plan to reduce the federal deficit.
He voted against the final report of the commission.
In 2012, Ryan accused the nation's top military leaders of using " ___E:smoke and mirrors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_and_mirrors)___ " to remain under budget limits passed by Congress.

Ryan later said that he misspoke on the issue and called ___E:General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_(United_States))___ ___E:Martin Dempsey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Dempsey)___ , the ___E:Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Joint_Chiefs_of_Staff)___ , to apologize for his comments.

___E:Dan Balz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Balz)___ of The Washington Post wrote that Ryan was promoted as a candidate for vice president "by major elements of the conservative opinion makers, including The Wall Street Journal editorial page, the Weekly Standard and the editor of National Review ".
On August 11, 2012, the Romney campaign announced Ryan as its choice for Vice President  through its "Mitt's VP" ___E:mobile app U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_app)___ .

It was reported that Romney had offered the position to Ryan on August 1, 2012,  the day after returning from a foreign policy trip to the United Kingdom, ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland)___ , and ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel)___ .

On August 11, 2012, Ryan formally accepted Romney's invitation to join his campaign as his running mate, in front of the ___E:USS Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Wisconsin_(BB-64))___ in Norfolk.

Ryan is the first individual from ___E:Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin)___  as well as the first member of ___E:Generation X U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_X)___  to run on a ___E:major party's national ticket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_major_party_presidential_tickets)___ .

Also in August 2012, the ___E:Associated Press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press)___ published a story saying that while the ___E:Tea Party movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_movement)___ had wanted a nominee other than Romney, it had gotten "one of its ideological heroes" in the vice presidential slot. According to the article, Ryan supports the Tea Party's belief in "individual rights, distrust of big government and an allegorical embrace of the Founding Fathers".

According to a statistical-historical analysis conducted by ___E:Nate Silver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Silver)___ , "Ryan is the most conservative Republican member of Congress to be picked for the vice-presidential slot since at least 1900" and "is also more conservative than any Democratic nominee [for vice president who previously served in the Congress] was liberal, meaning that he is the furthest from the center" of any vice presidential candidate chosen from Congress since the turn of the 20th century.

Political scientist Eric Schickler commented that while Ryan "may well be the most conservative vice presidential nominee in decades," the NOMINATE methodology "is not suited to making claims about the relative liberalism or conservatism of politicians" over a long time span.  A USA Today / ___E:Gallup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gallup_Organization)___ poll found that 39% thought Ryan was an "excellent" or "pretty good" vice presidential choice, compared to 42% who felt he was a "fair" or "poor" choice.

Ryan formally accepted his nomination at the ___E:2012 Republican National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Republican_National_Convention)___ on August 29, 2012.  In his acceptance speech, he promoted ___E:Mitt Romney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney)___ as the presidential candidate, supported repeal of the ___E:Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act)___ (PPACA),  said that he and Romney had a plan to generate 12 million new jobs over the ensuing four years, and promoted founding principles as a solution: "We will not duck the tough issues—we will lead. We will not spend four years blaming others—we will take responsibility.
We will not try to replace our founding principles, we will reapply our founding principles."
The speech was well received by the convention audience and praised for being well-delivered.
Some fact-checkers purported that there were important factual omissions and that he presented details out of context.

Conservative media (including ___E:Jennifer Rubin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Rubin_(journalist))___ of The Washington Post ,  the Investor's Business Daily ,  and ___E:Fox News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News)___  ) disputed some of the fact-checkers' findings.

Of 33 of Ryan's statements which Politifact.com suspected of being false or misleading, it rated 10.5% as True, 18% as Mostly True, 21% as Half True, 36% as Mostly False, 9% as False, and 6% as Pants on Fire.  On October 11, 2012, Ryan debated his Democratic counterpart, incumbent Vice President ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ , in ___E:the only vice presidential debate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election_debates,_2012)___ of the 2012 election cycle.
Romney and Ryan lost the 2012 presidential election, but Ryan retained his seat in the House of Representatives.
On September 25, 2015, ___E:John Boehner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner)___ formally announced to House Republicans his intention to resign from the speakership and the House.

Among those interested in the post, ___E:Kevin McCarthy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_McCarthy)___ —who had wide support among Republicans, including Boehner, and Ryan, who was set to officially nominate him—was considered the presumptive favorite.

His candidacy was opposed by conservative House Republicans of the ___E:Freedom Caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Caucus)___ , and when it became clear that caucus members would not support his candidacy, McCarthy withdrew his name from consideration on October 8. This led many Republicans to turn to Ryan as a compromise candidate.
The push included a plea from Boehner, who reportedly told Ryan that he was the only person who could unite the House Republicans at a time of turmoil.

Ryan released a statement that said, "While I am grateful for the encouragement I've received, I will not be a candidate."  The next day however, close aides of Ryan's confirmed that Ryan had re-evaluated the situation, and was considering the possibility of a run.

Ryan confirmed on October 22, that he would seek the speakership after receiving the endorsements of two factions of House Republicans, including the conservative ___E:Freedom Caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Caucus)___ .
Ryan, upon confirming his bid for the speakership, stated, "I never thought I'd be speaker.

But I pledged to you that if I could be a unifying figure, then I would serve – I would go all in. After talking with so many of you, and hearing your words of encouragement, I believe we are ready to move forward as one, united team. And I am ready and eager to be our speaker."

On October 29, Ryan was elected Speaker, receiving 236 votes, an ___E:absolute majority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermajority#Majority_of_the_entire_membership)___ of the 435-member chamber. ___E:Democrat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:Nancy Pelosi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi)___ received 184 votes, with 12 more going to others.

After the vote Ryan delivered his first remarks as speaker-elect and was ___E:sworn in U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oath_of_office#Federal_executive_and_legislative_branch_oaths)___ by ___E:John Conyers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Conyers)___ , the ___E:dean of the House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ , becoming, at age 45, the youngest person elected as speaker since ___E:James G. Blaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine)___ (age 39) in 1869.   Later, he named lobbyist ___E:John David Hoppe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_David_Hoppe)___ as his ___E:chief of staff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_staff)___ .
Ryan became the leader of the House Republicans upon becoming Speaker.
However, by tradition, he largely stopped taking part in debate and made only a few votes from the floor.
He was also not a member of any committees.

After ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ became the presumptive Republican nominee in the 2016 presidential election on May 4, 2016, Ryan was hesitant to endorse him, stating on May 5 that he was "not ready".

Ryan and Trump met in private on May 12, releasing a joint statement afterward, acknowledging their differences but stating "we recognize that there are also many important areas of common ground."  On June 2, Ryan announced his support for Trump in an op-ed in The Janesville Gazette .

The following day, June 3, amid Trump's criticism of Judge ___E:Gonzalo P. Curiel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonzalo_P._Curiel)___ , Ryan said Trump's critique "just was out of left field for my mind," and voiced disagreement with him.  On June 7, Ryan disavowed Trump's comments about Curiel because he believed they were "the textbook definition of a racist comment".

Nevertheless, Ryan continued to endorse Trump, believing that more Republican policies will be enacted under Donald Trump than presumptive Democratic nominee ___E:Hillary Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton)___ .

On June 15, after ___E:Kevin McCarthy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_McCarthy)___ stated during a conversation among Republicans, "There's two people I think ___E:Putin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin)___ pays: ___E:Rohrabacher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Rohrabacher)___ and Trump.
Swear to God", Ryan interjected, "No leaks.
This is how we know we're a real family here."

On July 5, after FBI Director ___E:James Comey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Comey)___ advocated against pressing charges against Clinton for her email scandal, Ryan said Comey's decision "defies explanation" and stated that "[d]eclining to prosecute Secretary Clinton for recklessly mishandling and transmitting national security information will set a terrible precedent."
During the 2016 presidential campaign, Ryan suggested that candidate Trump should release his tax returns.

In October 2016, following the ___E:Donald Trump Access Hollywood controversy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Access_Hollywood_controversy)___ , Ryan disinvited Trump from a scheduled campaign rally,  and announced that he would no longer defend or support Trump's presidential campaign but would focus instead on Congressional races.

He also freed down-ticket congress members to use their own judgment about Trump, saying "you all need to do what's best for you and your district."  Trump then went on to attack Ryan, accusing him and other "disloyal" Republicans of deliberately undermining his candidacy as part of "a whole sinister deal".

Two months after the ___E:2016 elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections)___ , Ryan was re-elected Speaker of the House on January 3, 2017, the opening day of the ___E:115th Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/115th_United_States_Congress)___ .
He received 239 votes to House Democratic Leader Pelosi's 189 votes (with 5 more going to others).

On February 7, 2017, Ryan told reporters a replacement for the Affordable Care Act (ACA) would be introduced "this year" amid speculation Donald Trump would not act toward doing so until the following year.  On March 9, Ryan gave a 30-minute lecture explaining the proposed replacement for the ACA, titled the ___E:American Health Care Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Health_Care_Act)___ (AHCA).

On March 30, Ryan said that he did not intend to work with Democrats on repealing and replacing the ACA, reasoning their involvement would lead to "government running health care."  On April 4, Ryan confirmed renewed discussions of an ACA replacement, but warned that a replacement was in the "conceptual" stages of its development.
On May 4, the House narrowly voted for the AHCA to repeal the ACA.  On May 9, Ryan said that "a month or two" would pass before the Senate would pass its own ACA repeal and replacement legislation.
The Senate created several of its own versions of the act but was unable to pass any of them.

In May 2017, Ryan said Congress' goal was "calendared 2017 for tax reform" and reported progress was being made in doing so.
